facts.statement: The genus Longipteryx was first described by Zhang and colleagues in 2001.
Longipteryx lived during the Early Cretaceous, specifically the Aptian stage, approximately 120.3 million years ago.
facts.quote: Longipteryx is a genus of prehistoric bird which lived during the Early Cretaceous (Aptian stage, 120.3 million years ago).

facts.statement: Fossils of Longipteryx were found in the Jiufotang Formation in Chaoyang, Liaoning Province, China.
facts.quote: Its remains have been recovered from the Jiufotang Formation at Chaoyang in Liaoning Province, China.

facts.statement: The name Longipteryx translates to "one with long feathers," derived from Latin and Ancient Greek roots.
facts.quote: The name Longipteryx means "one with long feathers", from Latin longus, "long" + Ancient Greek pteryx (πτέρυξ), "wing", "feather" or "pinion".

facts.statement: Longipteryx possessed a long snout that was longer than the rest of its head, ending in a few hooked teeth.
facts.quote: It had a long snout — longer than the rest of the head — with a few hooked teeth at the tip

facts.statement: Unlike most birds of its time, Longipteryx possessed uncinate processes that strengthened its ribcage.
facts.quote: unlike most other birds of its time it possessed uncinate processes which strengthened the ribcage

facts.statement: The humerus of Longipteryx was 1.56 times the length of its femur.
facts.quote: the humerus was 1.56 times the length of the femur

facts.statement: The holotype preserves impressions of body feathers, wing coverts, and down, but lacks preserved flight feathers (remiges).
facts.quote: The holotype retains many feather impressions, though poorly preserved; remiges do not seem to have been preserved, and what feathers remain are apparently only body feathers, wing coverts and down.

facts.statement: The absence of long tail display feathers in all known specimens suggests that Longipteryx did not possess them.
facts.quote: the absence of such feathers in any known specimen of Longipteryx probably indicates that they were absent in this species

facts.statement: Longipteryx was initially interpreted by researchers as a piscivore or insectivore before evidence for frugivory was found.
facts.quote: Initially, it was interpreted as a piscivore or an insectivore.

facts.statement: In life, Longipteryx measured approximately 15 cm in length, excluding the tail.
facts.quote: En vida, Longipteryx medía cerca de 15 cm, excluyendo la cola.

facts.statement: A distinct order, Longipterygiformes, and family, Longipterygidae, have been proposed for Longipteryx.
facts.quote: A distinct order (Longipterygiformes) and family (Longipterygidae) has been proposed for it.

facts.statement: Longipteryx is sometimes included in the clade Enantiornithes, specifically within Euenantiornithes, while other analyses classify it as basal to Enantiornithes.
facts.quote: En ocasiones se le incluye en el clado Enantiornithes, concretamente en el grupo Euenantiornithes, mientras que en otros análisis el género es clasificado como basal en Enantiornithes o respecto a este grupo.

facts.statement: The discovery of Longirostravis, which is closely related to Longipteryx, led researchers to suggest they form a specialized group of Euenantiornithes.
facts.quote: Años después fue descrita otra ave similar, Longirostravis, cuya relación con Longipteryx era más próxima que la de otras aves conocidas, lo que llevó a pensar que estas aves formaban un grupo especializado de euenantiornites.

facts.statement: In 2026, Clark and colleagues described two new specimens of Longipteryx chaoyangensis that provided the best-preserved plumage and the first evidence of wing shape for the species.
facts.quote: Clark et al. (2026) describe two new specimens of Longipteryx chaoyangensis with the best-preserved plumage reported to date and providing the first evidence of wing shape of the studied birds.
